Savvy

SAV-ee — a savvy person 'has' the practical know-how to handle things well. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Savvy is shrewd and knowledgeable, especially about practical matters.

The savvy negotiator knew exactly when to walk away from the table to get a better deal.

Worked Example

Before buying a used car, a shopper researches its exact model online, checks its full repair history, and brings a mechanic friend along to inspect the engine before ever speaking to the salesperson.

Being practically knowledgeable enough to avoid getting cheated is exactly what it means to be savvy. Unlike 'lucky,' which is about chance, savvy is about genuine skill and awareness.

How Savvy Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

shrewd

shrewd: having sharp judgment, especially in practical matters

astute

astute: having keen judgment or insight

canny

canny: clever and cautious, especially about money or deals

Antonyms

naive

naive: lacking experience or worldly wisdom

clueless

clueless: having no understanding or awareness

How Strong Is It? — informed → shrewd → savvy

informed vs. savvy

informed vs. savvy: Informed is weaker than savvy — being informed just means you have facts, while being savvy means you know how to use that knowledge cleverly in practical situations.

shrewd vs. savvy

shrewd vs. savvy: Shrewd can feel sharper than savvy: both describe practical smarts, but shrewd often implies an even sharper, sometimes calculating edge to that knowledge.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — sav-/sap-

root — sav-/sap-: to know, to be wise (Latin (sapere), via French/Creole savez)

Put it together

Put it together: Savvy traces back to Latin sapere, 'to be wise, to know,' passed into English through a French/Creole phrase meaning 'you know.' At its root, being savvy means genuinely knowing what you're doing.

Use the root in a new word: sage

Use the root in a new word: sage: The old sage offered calm advice to every traveler who visited her cottage.
